questions.q: What is the main trade-off a preferred shareholder accepts compared to a common shareholder?
options: Preferred shareholders get voting rights but no dividend
Preferred shareholders get a fixed, priority dividend and liquidation priority, but typically no voting rights
Preferred shareholders can never receive any payout at all
Preferred shareholders automatically become company directors
questions.explain: Preferred stock is paid a fixed dividend before common shareholders and has priority in liquidation, but in exchange usually carries no voting rights and doesn't share in the company's upside the way common stock does.

questions.q: A company announces a 2-for-1 stock split. What happens to the total market value of an investor's holding immediately after the split?
options: It doubles, because they now have twice as many shares
It is cut in half, because the price per share is halved
It stays the same — twice the shares at half the price per share
It becomes impossible to determine without a dividend adjustment
questions.explain: A stock split multiplies share count and divides price per share by the same factor, leaving total market value unchanged.

questions.q: How does a share buyback affect remaining shareholders?
options: It dilutes them by issuing more shares
It has no effect on share count at all
It reduces the number of shares outstanding, so each remaining share represents a claim on more of the company's earnings
It converts common stock into preferred stock
questions.explain: A buyback uses company cash to repurchase and retire shares. With fewer shares outstanding dividing the same profit, each remaining share represents a larger claim on earnings.

options: Two companies merging into a single new company
A company separating part of its business into a new, independently traded company, distributing its shares to existing shareholders
A company issuing additional common shares to raise cash
A company converting all its preferred stock into common stock
questions.explain: A spin-off separates part of a business into a new, independently traded entity, and existing shareholders of the parent receive shares of the new company.

questions.q: Why do historical stock price datasets include an "adjusted close" price alongside the raw close?
options: Adjusted close reflects only intraday trading, not end-of-day prices
Adjusted close removes artificial jumps caused by splits, dividends, and other corporate actions so historical analysis isn't distorted
Adjusted close is simply the price rounded to the nearest dollar
Adjusted close only applies to preferred stock, not common stock
questions.explain: Corporate actions like splits change the raw price without reflecting any real change in the business. Adjusted prices rescale history backward so these events don't create misleading price jumps.
